interaction.content: Hello, Samantha. It's nice to meet you. How can I assist you today?
Hi. I have this fear that's been eating away at me for a while now. I'm scared of breaking my leg while playing tennis, and it's really affecting my life.
That sounds very distressing. Can you tell me more about when this fear started and what you notice when you experience it?
It started a few months ago after I had a minor sprain during a match. Since then, every time I step onto the court, I get anxious that I'll break my leg and never play again.
I see. So, this fear arose after that sprain. Have there been any specific instances or incidents that have intensified this fear since then?
Yeah, every minor strain or awkward movement just seems to make it worse. It's like, even if nothing serious happens, I still feel on edge.
That's understandable. It sounds like these thoughts are quite persistent. How has this fear impacted your ability to play tennis and enjoy the game?
It's made playing tennis really unenjoyable. I'm always super cautious and I can’t focus. It’s affecting my performance and it’s frustrating because tennis used to be something I loved.
It must be really frustrating to have something you love so deeply affected. When you say you're cautious, what kinds of things do you find yourself doing or avoiding?
I try not to push myself too hard, and I avoid certain moves that I think might cause an injury. But no matter how careful I am, the fear doesn’t go away.
That must feel very limiting. Have you noticed any effects on other areas of your life, such as your sleep patterns or your interactions with friends?
Yeah, my sleep has been pretty disturbed. I keep thinking about "what if it happens tomorrow." And with my tennis friends, they’ve noticed I’m not myself on the court because I’m always worried.
It sounds like this fear has a broad impact on your well-being. Have you discussed these concerns with anyone in your support system?
Not really. I have a close friend who I could talk to, but I haven’t brought it up. I’m not sure they’d understand.

Sometimes it can be challenging to open up about these fears, especially if you're unsure how others will react. What are your thoughts on exploring the source of these fears and testing their reality together in our sessions?
I guess it could be helpful. I just don’t know if talking about it will make the fear go away.
It's completely okay to feel unsure. Part of what we can do here is assess the basis of these fears and see if they hold up when we look at them closely. How does that sound?
I guess it can’t hurt to try. I’m just tired of feeling like this all the time.

It's understandable to feel that way. Let's start by discussing some safety measures you can take while playing, to perhaps reduce this fear a bit. Have you ever considered or tried any specific precautions?
I’ve thought about wearing extra protective gear, but I’m not sure it’d make a difference. The fear isn’t really rational, I know that much.
It's good that you're aware of that. What if we also focused on the positive experiences you've had on the court? Can you recall any recent moments where you felt good or enjoyed playing tennis?
Well, there was this one match last week where I forgot about my fear for a bit. I hit a really great shot, and it felt like old times.
That sounds wonderful. Those moments are important to remember. Do you think keeping those positive experiences in mind might help balance your thoughts when fear tries to take over?
Maybe. It's hard to stay focused on the good when the fear feels so immediate, but I suppose it’s worth a try.
It's definitely worth exploring. We might also try some small, structured experiments where you gradually face these fears and see what actually happens. Does that sound manageable?
I guess I can give it a shot. I do want to get back to enjoying tennis like I used to.
That's a great start. Between now and our next session, would you be willing to note down any fears that come up while playing and also any positive moments, no matter how small?
Sure, I can do that. It might help to see things written down.
Excellent. We'll review those observations together next time. Take things at your own pace, and remember, it's about gradual progress. We'll tackle this step by step.
Okay, that sounds fair. Thank you. I'll try my best.
You're welcome, Samantha. We'll work through this together. Looking forward to our next session. Take care until then.

interaction.content: Hi Jason, I'm glad you decided to come in today. Can you tell me a bit about what's been going on that's made you seek out counseling?
Hi. Well, I’ve been feeling like I can't cook well enough. It's been especially tough recently after I got a negative review on one of my dishes at work.
That sounds really challenging. How long have you been feeling this way about your cooking?
It's been a few years, but the intensity of these feelings has really ramped up over the past few months.
I see. Can you pinpoint what might have caused this escalation in your feelings of inadequacy?
Honestly, it’s my perfectionism. I have such high expectations for myself, and when things don’t turn out perfectly, I feel like a failure. The negative review just made everything worse.
Perfectionism can be a tough mindset to break. How do these feelings of inadequacy affect your daily life and work as a chef?
It’s pretty bad. I constantly doubt my abilities, and it's affecting my job performance. My relationships with my colleagues are strained because I'm so focused on getting everything perfect.
It sounds like there’s a lot of pressure you’re putting on yourself. When a dish doesn’t turn out the way you want, what kinds of thoughts go through your mind?
I start thinking that I'm not a good cook and that maybe I don’t have what it takes to be successful in this field. It just spirals from there.
Those must be really difficult thoughts to deal with. When you do receive positive feedback, how does that affect your feelings about your cooking?
For a moment, it feels good, but it doesn’t last long. I quickly go back to critiquing myself and focusing on the next dish that needs to be perfect.
It seems like you have a tendency to discount the positives quickly. Has anyone in your support system been helpful during these times?
I do have a few close friends, but I find it hard to talk about these specific feelings with them. They don’t really understand the pressure I put on myself in the kitchen.

It’s great that you have close friends, even if discussing your feelings is challenging right now. Besides perfectionism, have you noticed any other patterns in your thoughts that contribute to your self-doubt?
Sometimes, I do think in extremes, like 'I either cook a perfect dish or I’m a terrible chef.' I guess I overgeneralize based on a single dish.
Recognizing that pattern is an important step. When you think back on your experiences in the kitchen, are there any moments you are particularly proud of?
There are a few dishes that turned out really well, and the customers loved them. But then I remember the negative comments and feel like those successes don’t matter as much.
It seems like you're filtering out the positives and focusing heavily on the negatives. Could it be helpful to keep a balanced view of your successes and areas for improvement?
I suppose it could, but it's hard. I've been doing this for so long, it feels like second nature.
Habits like these can be tough to shift, but it's definitely possible. Would you be open to exploring some ways to reframe your self-judgments to find a more balanced perspective?
I’m willing to try. I really want to enjoy cooking again and not feel like a failure all the time.
That's a great start. Let’s begin by identifying specific negative thoughts and working to challenge them. How does that sound?
It sounds good. I think being aware of these thoughts might help me start changing them.
Excellent. We can also work on recognizing when you’re overgeneralizing and mental filtering. Practicing more balanced thinking can be a significant shift.
Alright, I’m on board. What do I need to do next?

Let’s start with a small task. This week, try to notice when you have a negative thought about your cooking. Write it down, and also note any positive feedback you receive. We’ll discuss it in our next session.
That sounds doable. I’ll give it a shot and see how it goes.
Perfect. Keep an open mind and pay attention to how you feel during this process. We’ll build on this as we go along. I’m looking forward to hearing about your progress next time.

interaction.content: Hi Harper, it’s nice to meet you. How are you feeling today?
Hi. I'm okay, I guess. Just a bit frustrated with myself.
I’m sorry to hear that you’re feeling frustrated. Can you tell me a little more about what’s been bothering you?
Well, I had this chess event last weekend. Overall, it went well, but I spilled water on myself during one of the games, and that just ruined everything for me.
That sounds like a difficult moment for you. It’s understandable that it feels significant. Can you tell me about some of the positive aspects of the event?
Sure. I played against some really strong opponents and even won a few games. I also learned a lot of new strategies, which was pretty cool.
It sounds like there were quite a few positives. What made the water spill stand out so much to you?
I guess it just made me feel really embarrassed. Everyone saw it, and I couldn't stop thinking about it, even though the other games went well.
It’s understandable to feel embarrassed in that moment. When you reflect on the event now, how much of your thoughts are focused on the spill versus the successful games you played?
Honestly, most of my thoughts are about the spill. It’s hard for me to focus on the victories when something went so wrong.
That makes sense. It sounds like the negative experience is overshading the positive ones for you. How do you usually handle situations when something doesn't go as planned?
I usually feel pretty down. I just keep thinking about what went wrong and how I could have avoided it.
It sounds like focusing on the negatives is something that tends to happen frequently. Have you noticed any impact this has had on your enjoyment of activities or experiences?
Yeah, it definitely makes it harder to enjoy things. Even when something goes well, I end up fixating on the one thing that didn't.

It’s really good that you’re aware of this pattern. Sometimes recognizing it is the first step to making a change. What do you think might help in shifting this focus from the negatives to the positives?
I'm not sure. Maybe if I tried to remind myself of the good things that happened? But it’s hard when my mind keeps going back to the bad stuff.

That’s a great start. Actively reminding yourself of the positives can be very helpful. What do you think about trying to write down the positive aspects of your experiences, like a journal or a list?
I think I could try that. It might help to see them written down and remind me that not everything went wrong.

That’s a wonderful idea. Having a physical list can serve as a strong reminder of the positives. Besides writing things down, are there other ways you think you could help yourself stay focused on positive aspects?
Maybe I could talk to my friends more about the good parts instead of just the bad stuff.
That sounds like a supportive step. Sharing positive experiences with friends can reinforce them in your mind. How do you usually feel when you share your successes with others?
It makes me feel good, like I'm not alone and that other people see the good things too.
That’s great to hear. Surrounding yourself with supportive people can really help balance your perspective. How do you think you can start incorporating these changes into your daily life?
I think I'll start with the journal idea. I'll write down at least three positive things from each day, even if something negative happens.

That sounds like a solid plan. Remember, it’s okay to acknowledge the negatives, but also give space for the positives. Is there anything else you’d like to explore or any support you need as you begin this process?
I think I just need to remind myself to keep it up regularly. Maybe setting a daily reminder to write in my journal?

That’s a smart approach. Setting a daily reminder can help make it a habit. How about we check in on your progress next time we meet? We can discuss how it’s working for you and make any adjustments if needed.
That sounds good. I’m feeling a bit more hopeful about this now.
I’m glad to hear that, Harper. It’s wonderful to see you being proactive about making positive changes. We’ll continue to build on this together. See you next time!

interaction.content: Hi Taylor, I'm glad you're here today. How are you feeling?
Hi, I'm feeling a bit nervous, to be honest. I've never done this before.
That's completely understandable. It's okay to feel nervous. We can take things at your own pace. Can you tell me a bit about what brought you here today?

Well, I’ve been struggling with feeling inadequate, especially when it comes to practical skills. My husband is in the military and usually handles things like changing tires. When he’s away, and I have to manage on my own, those tasks feel overwhelming.
It sounds like you’ve been under a lot of stress, especially with your husband being away. Can you tell me more about a recent situation where these feelings were particularly strong?

Sure, a few weeks ago, I got a flat tire. It took me forever to change it, and I just felt so helpless and frustrated. It made me question my ability to handle anything like that, especially with a baby on the way.
That must have been an incredibly challenging experience for you. How did you feel once you managed to change the tire?

I mean, I was relieved it was done, but I still felt like such a failure. It shouldn’t have taken me so long. I just kept thinking, if I can't manage simple things, how am I going to take care of a baby?
It's understandable to feel that way, especially with so much on your mind. When these thoughts come up about your abilities, what kind of things do you find yourself saying to yourself?
Mostly that I'm useless and that I’ll never be able to handle anything on my own. It’s like, if I can’t do something as basic as changing a tire, how am I supposed to be a good mom?
Those are very strong and heavy thoughts. How do these thoughts impact your day-to-day activities and your overall mood?
They really get me down. I end up avoiding tasks that seem too hard or I procrastinate because I’m scared of failing again. It’s exhausting and it makes me feel like I can’t do anything right.
It sounds like these thoughts are really affecting your confidence and your daily life. Have you talked to anyone about how you’re feeling?
Not really. My husband is supportive, but he's not here much, and I don’t want to worry him. I’m afraid to talk to my family about it because I don’t think they’d understand or they might judge me.

It sounds like you're feeling quite isolated in this. I'm glad you decided to reach out for some support here. Let's start by looking more closely at those thoughts you mentioned. Can you think of any times when you successfully handled a challenging situation?
Hmm, well... I guess there were a few times I figured things out on my own, like fixing small things around the house. But those didn’t feel as significant as the tire incident.

It’s important to recognize all of your successes, big and small. Those moments show that you are capable. How do you think it would feel to shift your focus a bit towards these successes when you start to have those negative thoughts?
I suppose it might make me feel a bit better. But it’s hard to ignore the bigger failures when they stick out so much.

It can be challenging to change our focus, but it’s a worthwhile practice. Every step counts, and celebrating your smaller achievements can build confidence over time. When you consider the tire incident, how much time and effort do you think you spent on it?
I don’t know exactly, but it took a lot longer than it should have. Maybe over an hour, and it felt like I was struggling the whole time.

It certainly sounds like it was a tough experience. But spending over an hour on something you weren’t familiar with also shows persistence and determination. Could we view that as a learning opportunity rather than a failure?
I guess I never thought of it that way. It did take a lot of effort, even if it wasn’t perfect.

That’s a great perspective. Viewing it as a learning experience can reduce some of the weight those negative thoughts carry. With practice, these changes can grow your confidence. How would you feel about exploring this more in our sessions?
I think I’d be open to that. I just want to feel better and not dread these tasks so much.

That’s a great start, Taylor. We’ll work together on this, and take it one step at a time. Today, you’ve already made significant progress by sharing your experiences and being open to new ways of thinking.

interaction.content: Hi Nathan, I'm glad you could make it today. How are you feeling right now?
Hi. I’m a bit overwhelmed, actually. I'm here because I've been struggling a lot with feelings of guilt and inadequacy recently.
I'm sorry to hear that you're feeling this way. Could you tell me more about what’s been going on and what’s triggered these feelings?
It all started last week when I forgot to give my students a pop quiz I had planned. Since then, I've been constantly blaming myself and feeling like I've let them down.
It sounds like missing that quiz has had a significant impact on you. Can you walk me through what happened and how you felt when you realized you’d forgotten?

Yeah, I was rushing through my lessons and just completely forgot about the quiz. When I remembered later, I felt this wave of panic and all these thoughts about being irresponsible and a failure came rushing in.
It seems like this event triggered some intense emotions and thoughts for you. How have these feelings been affecting your day-to-day life?

It's been rough. I can't stop thinking about it. I keep replaying the situation in my head and thinking about how my students must feel about me now. It’s affecting my sleep and even my teaching because I feel so distracted and guilty.
That sounds exhausting, dealing with such constant negative thoughts. Have you noticed any specific patterns or common themes in the way you think about this situation?
Yeah, I guess I always jump to the worst-case scenario. Like, I assume my students are all thinking I'm incompetent, and that I’ve ruined their chances to succeed.
So, you often find yourself imagining the worst possible outcomes. Do these thoughts seem logical to you when you look at them closely?
Honestly, they do in the moment. But then I catch myself and think maybe I'm overreacting. But the guilt just won’t go away.

It’s good that you can recognize when you might be overreacting. Let's explore how accurate some of those thoughts may be. What evidence do you have that supports the idea that your students think you’re incompetent?
Well, none of them have outright said anything. But, I just feel like they might be disappointed or losing trust in me. I don’t know, it’s just a gut feeling.
That’s understandable. It's common to feel uncertain after something like this. What about any evidence that contradicts those thoughts, anything positive since the incident?
Hmm, I guess some of my students have done well on their assignments. And no one has complained or mentioned the missed quiz, which might mean they didn’t think much of it.
That’s an important observation. It suggests that the situation might not be as catastrophic as it feels in your mind. How do these realizations make you feel?
It feels a little relieving, but I still can’t shake off the guilt completely. What if I've overlooked something? What if they’re just being polite and actually are disappointed?
Those 'what if' thoughts can be quite persistent. Let's think about the real impact of missing that quiz. How crucial was it to your students’ overall progress?
It was just a pop quiz meant to gauge their understanding, not a major exam. They can still show their knowledge in other assignments and the extra credit I gave them.
It sounds like the actual educational impact might be minimal. Given that, how might you reframe your thoughts about missing the quiz?
I guess I could try to see it as just a small mistake, not something that ruins everything. Maybe the extra credit can even help them a bit more.
That’s a helpful reframe. Mistakes happen, and it’s important to recognize our efforts to make up for them. What can you do next time to remind yourself of this balanced perspective?
Maybe I can focus on the positives, like the extra credit, and remind myself that one small mistake doesn’t define my abilities as a teacher.

It sounds like a plan. I’m still skeptical, but I’ll give it a shot. Anything to stop feeling this way.
That's all we can ask for—to try and see how things evolve. We’ll continue to explore these patterns and develop effective coping strategies together. You're not alone in this, Nathan.

interaction.content: Hi Cody, welcome. I'm glad you're here. How are you feeling today?
Hi. I'm okay, I guess. A bit anxious about this session, if I'm honest.
That's completely understandable. Starting something new can often bring up feelings of anxiety. Is there a particular reason you're seeking counseling today?
Yeah, I quit my job to travel and work on a cryptocurrency project, and it's been weighing heavily on me. I feel insecure and full of self-doubt about my decision.
It sounds like making such a significant change has been challenging for you. Can you tell me a bit more about what led you to make this decision?
I've always been fascinated by cryptocurrency and felt that I needed a change. My job was stable, but it didn't make me happy. I thought taking this leap would be exciting and fulfilling.
It's quite brave to follow your passions and seek fulfillment in your career. Since you've made this change, what sorts of feelings have you been experiencing?
Mainly insecurity and self-doubt. I'm constantly worried about what my old coworkers think about me leaving. They probably think I was foolish to leave such a stable job.
It sounds like you're concerned with how others might be perceiving your decision, which is a lot of pressure to carry. Have these feelings been consistent since you left your job?
Pretty much, yeah. They started right after I left, and they've only gotten worse over time.
I see. How have these feelings impacted other areas of your life, like your travels or your new project?
My focus and productivity have definitely suffered. I'm also finding it hard to really enjoy my travels or the work I'm doing because I'm constantly second-guessing myself.
That must be really tough, feeling like these doubts are overshadowing the new experiences you're having. Have you had a chance to talk to anyone about how you're feeling?
Not really. I have a close friend who's supportive, but I haven't told them about my insecurity. I just don't want to burden them with my problems.
It's good that you have someone supportive in your life. Often sharing our struggles with trusted people can be very helpful. How do you think your friend might respond if you did open up to them?
They'd probably be supportive and remind me why I made the decision in the first place, but I still feel hesitant. It's embarrassing to admit I'm doubting myself this much.

It's okay to feel hesitant. Many people feel vulnerable opening up about their inner struggles. Given what you're experiencing, it might be helpful to explore some of the specific thoughts that contribute to your self-doubt. Would you be comfortable doing that?
Sure, I can try. I guess a lot of it revolves around thinking I’ve made a huge mistake and that my coworkers are judging me for it.
Let's unpack that a bit. What makes you think your coworkers are judging you negatively?
Well, I haven't spoken to them since I left, so I don't know for sure. But I just can't shake this feeling that they're talking behind my back, saying I was stupid to leave.
It sounds like you're imagining the worst-case scenario about what they might be thinking. Has there been any evidence that confirms your fears?
Not really. It's more like an assumption I've made. But it's hard not to imagine that's what's happening.

It can indeed be challenging to move past our assumptions, especially when we're feeling vulnerable. If we were to think of a different perspective, what might be an alternative way to view their potential reactions?
Maybe... maybe some of them could actually admire me for taking a risk? I mean, it's not like everyone is happy with their jobs, even if they seem stable.
That's a very valuable perspective. It's important to consider that their reaction might not be as negative as you fear. How does thinking about it in this way change how you feel?
It makes me feel a bit better, but there's still that nagging doubt. What if they really do think I'm an idiot?

It's completely natural for doubts to linger, even when we consider alternative perspectives. With time and practice, these new ways of thinking can become more natural and might help reduce that nagging doubt. How do you think you might reinforce this more balanced perspective in your daily life?
I guess I could try reminding myself why I made this decision and that taking risks is part of pursuing something important to me. Maybe keeping a journal of my thoughts could help too.
Those are excellent strategies. Keeping a journal can help you track your thoughts and revisit these more balanced perspectives. How does that idea sound to you?
It sounds good. I like the idea of writing things down and reflecting on them later.

Great. Let's plan to incorporate some journaling into your routine. It might also be helpful to practice thinking about how you would respond to any doubts or worries when they come up. How do you feel about using our sessions to explore these approaches further?
I think that could be really helpful. I'm open to trying it out.

interaction.content: Hello, Wanda. How are you feeling today?
Hi. I'm doing okay, I guess. Thanks for seeing me.
It's my pleasure, Wanda. How can I assist you today?
Well, lately, I've been struggling with feeling inadequate and unsuccessful in my career. It's been really tough.
I'm sorry to hear that. Could you tell me more about when these feelings started and what you think might be contributing to them?

They started about a year ago. I play baseball professionally, and I make good money, but I just can't shake the feeling that my degree from Miami University isn't prestigious enough for a good job outside of baseball.
That sounds like it's been weighing heavily on you. Have these feelings affected other aspects of your life as well?
Yes, definitely. My performance on the field has suffered, and my relationships with my colleagues aren't great either. It's even affected my sleep and self-care routines.
It sounds like these thoughts have had a significant impact on various areas of your life. When you faced unsuccessful job applications, how did that influence your thinking about your education?
It just reinforced my belief that my degree isn't good enough. I keep thinking that if I had gone to a more prestigious school, things would be different.
I see. It's common for our thoughts to influence how we feel and act. How do these thoughts about your education usually make you feel?
They make me feel pretty low, like I'm not good enough or successful despite everything I've accomplished.
That sounds really challenging, Wanda. What have you tried doing to manage or change these thoughts on your own?
I've tried to tell myself that it's not true and that I've done well for myself, but it doesn't seem to have much effect.
It can be tough to challenge long-held beliefs on your own. During our sessions, we'll focus on exploring these thoughts more deeply and testing their validity. How does that sound to you?
I guess it sounds okay. I'm willing to try anything at this point.
Great. To start, let's think about a recent situation where you felt inadequate. Can you describe an instance that stands out to you?
Sure. Last week, I applied for a job in sports management. I didn't even get a callback, and it made me feel like I wasn't qualified enough.
That sounds really disheartening. When you didn't get the callback, what kind of thoughts went through your mind?
I thought that I must not be good enough and that they probably laughed at my qualifications.
Those thoughts sound really painful. What evidence do you have that supports the idea that you're not qualified?
Well, I didn't get the job, and it wasn't the first time. I've faced rejections before.
Rejections can indeed feel like proof, but let's consider this: what evidence is there that contradicts the idea that you're not qualified?
I guess I have played baseball at a high level, and I've managed a team in various capacities before. But it still feels like that's not enough.

It's important to consider all aspects of your experience. As we move forward, we'll look at these thoughts from different angles. Would you be open to setting up a small experiment to test these beliefs about your qualifications?
Yeah, I can try that. What kind of experiment are you thinking?
We could start by gathering some feedback from either colleagues or professionals in the field about your qualifications. This might help us see how others view your skills and experiences.
I guess I can do that. It might be helpful to get an outside perspective.
Excellent. Let's make a plan for how you'll go about gathering this feedback. How do you feel about reaching out to a few trusted colleagues or mentors?
I think I could do that. It'll be a bit uncomfortable, but I'm willing to give it a shot.
That's a great attitude, Wanda. After you gather the feedback, we can discuss what you find out and see how it aligns with your current thoughts about your qualifications. How does that sound?
Sounds like a plan. I'm curious to see what they'll say.
Wonderful. We'll take it one step at a time, and I'll be here to support you through the process. Is there anything else you want to discuss today?

interaction.content: Hi Cody, it's nice to meet you. How are you feeling about being here today?
Hi, it's nice to meet you too. Honestly, I'm a bit anxious and unsure about all this. Not entirely convinced it will help, but I'm here to try.
It's completely normal to feel that way, especially when starting something new. Can you tell me a bit about what brought you here today?

Sure. I've been struggling with OCD for a while now. It started in my teens but has gotten worse recently. It's really affecting my daily life and my relationships. My friends encouraged me to seek help because they noticed how much it’s impacting me.
That sounds like a lot to manage on your own. What kind of situations tend to trigger your OCD behaviors the most?
Mostly situations where I feel a lack of control or uncertainty. For example, if I’m not absolutely sure about something at work, I end up obsessively checking and double-checking everything.
It sounds like the need for control is a significant factor for you. How do you feel this need for control impacts your ability to trust positive feedback or gestures?
I guess I just don’t believe them. Like, when my students or colleagues give me a compliment, I think they’re just trying to be nice or don’t really mean it. I dismiss it almost automatically.

Dismissing positive feedback must reinforce those obsessive thoughts and make it hard to feel secure in those moments. Have you noticed any patterns or specific thoughts that come up when you receive positive feedback?
Yeah, I always think something like “they’re just saying that because they feel they have to” or “they don’t really mean it.” It’s hard to shake those thoughts off.
I understand. It can be tough when those thoughts feel automatic and persistent. Can you recall a recent instance where you received positive feedback and how you responded to it?

Yeah, just last week, one of my students’ parents sent a thank-you note for helping their child improve in reading. I immediately thought they were just being polite and didn’t see it as genuine appreciation.
That does sound challenging. Let’s explore that instance a bit more. What evidence did you have that suggested the parent’s note was insincere?
Well, I didn't really have any evidence. It’s just a feeling I get—that I can’t trust those kinds of positive gestures.
So, there wasn't solid evidence that the note wasn't sincere. Have there been times when feedback or gestures from others were sincere and well-meaning, but you doubted them anyway?
Yes, plenty of times, honestly. Even when people go out of their way to show appreciation, I still doubt it. It’s like my mind blocks the possibility that they truly mean it.
It sounds like these automatic doubts are quite ingrained. What do you think would happen if you accepted the feedback or gestures as genuine, even just for a moment?
I’m not really sure. Maybe I’d feel better about myself, but it’d be hard to believe it’s real. It’s like I’m protecting myself from potential disappointment or deceit.
Protecting yourself from disappointment makes sense, given your experiences. However, do you think this protective mechanism might also be limiting positive experiences and interactions for you?
Yeah, I guess it does. It’s like I’m stuck in a loop where I never fully enjoy or believe in the good things that happen because I’m always doubting them.

That makes a lot of sense. Maybe we can experiment with breaking that loop. How would you feel about, in future instances of positive feedback, testing the validity of your doubts by looking at evidence that both supports and contradicts them?
It sounds a bit challenging, but I’m open to trying. It’s better than being stuck in this cycle and constantly feeling doubtful.

Great, I'm glad you're open to it. How about we start by identifying one small, manageable instance to practice this with? Perhaps the next time you receive positive feedback, you could take a moment to consider the evidence for and against it being genuine?
Yeah, I think I can do that. It might be tough at first, but I'll try to give it a fair shot.
That's all we can ask for—a fair shot. It might also be helpful to keep track of these instances and what you find. Would you be willing to jot them down in a journal?
Sure, I can write them down. I think that could help me see things more clearly over time.
Excellent. This journal could serve as a tool to reflect on your thoughts and the evidence you gather. It can help us identify patterns and gradually challenge those automatic doubts.
That sounds like a good plan. I’m willing to give it a try and see how it goes.
It’s a good first step, Cody. We’ll take it one piece at a time. Remember, progress comes with patience and persistence. I’m glad that we’re starting this journey together.

interaction.content: Hello Ruth, I'm glad you could join us today. How are you feeling about starting this session?
Honestly, I'm not sure what I'm supposed to expect. I don't know if any of this will actually help me.
It's completely normal to feel uncertain at the beginning. Can you tell me a bit about what led you to seek counseling?
Well, I've been feeling lonely and full of self-doubt for a long time. I haven't dated since high school, and I think it's because guys find me unattractive.
That sounds really difficult. You've mentioned that you have these feelings of loneliness and self-doubt. When do you typically experience them most strongly?
Mostly when I'm around other people, especially in social situations where there might be a potential romantic interest. It just feels like everyone can see right through me.
It sounds like these feelings have been quite pervasive. Can you recall a recent situation where you felt this way? What was going through your mind?
There was this event a few weeks ago. I was at a friend's gathering, and this guy started talking to me. I could just tell by his body language and how he looked at me that he wasn’t interested.
That must have been really tough. When you say you could tell by his body language and look, what specific things were you noticing?
He kept looking around the room and not making much eye contact. It just felt like he was trying to find an excuse to move away.
What sort of thoughts did you have about yourself in that moment?
Just that I'm unattractive. I guess that's why I've been single all these years.
It sounds like those thoughts bring a lot of pain. Can we explore what evidence you might have to support or contradict these thoughts?
Evidence? It's not like I can prove he wasn’t interested. I just knew.
I understand. Sometimes, our minds can jump to conclusions without us realizing it. How often do you find yourself assuming what others think about you in these situations?
Almost always. It feels like second nature by now.
That’s understandable. What do you think might happen if we looked at these situations from a different angle? Maybe considering other explanations for their behavior?
I guess we could try. But I doubt it would change much. I've been feeling this way for so long.

It's definitely a challenge, especially when these patterns have been there for years. Let's start small. Can you think of any other reasons why someone might not make eye contact or look around the room?
Maybe he was just shy or nervous himself? But that seems unlikely.

It's a possibility. Sometimes people have their own reasons for how they act, unrelated to us. What do you think about experimenting with these ideas in real-life situations? Like testing if your assumptions hold true.
You want me to test if other people are really as disinterested as I think they are? How do I even do that?

We could start by observing interactions closely and noting down our thoughts and feelings about them. Maybe keeping a journal where you write these observations could help us identify patterns and themes over time.
I guess writing things down wouldn't hurt. But I'm still skeptical.

It's okay to feel skeptical. This process is gradual and about exploration. We’re not trying to force a change but rather to see if there are other ways to interpret these situations. Do you think you’d be willing to give it a try?
I suppose so. I’ll try writing things down, at least. Maybe it’ll help to see things from a different perspective.

That's a great start, Ruth. Remember, it’s about small steps. We’ll work together to understand and challenge these patterns. How about we begin by setting a goal for this week? Maybe noting down instances where you feel these self-doubts creep in?
Alright. I’ll try to keep track of when I feel this way and what I’m thinking. Hopefully, it helps.

Excellent. We'll review what you write in our next session. If you encounter any specific situations or need to discuss anything sooner, remember you can always bring it up. Thank you for being open to this process, Ruth.
Thanks. We'll see how it goes, I guess.

That must be really hard to deal with every day. When these negative thoughts come up, how do they affect your actions or your mood?
They make me feel hopeless. I avoid studying because I think it’s pointless, and I’ve kind of shut myself off from my friends and family. It just feels like I’m stuck in this dark place.

It seems like the thoughts you’re having about your future are really impacting your day-to-day life. Can you recall a recent moment where you experienced a strong negative reaction to a challenging situation?
Yeah, just the other day, I had another big test coming up, and I couldn’t even bring myself to study for it. I kept thinking, “What’s the use? I’m going to fail anyway.”
That sounds really frustrating. Let’s explore what specifically led to those thoughts. Can you walk me through what happened step-by-step?

Well, I sat down to study, opened my notes, and instantly felt this wave of panic. All I could think about was how badly I did on the last test and that it was going to happen again. Eventually, I just gave up and watched TV to distract myself.

Thank you for sharing that. It’s clear that the fear of failure really takes over in those moments. Have you noticed whether there’s any evidence supporting these thoughts that you’ll continue to fail, or counter-evidence that might suggest otherwise?
I mean, I did bad on this one test, so that’s definitely supporting it. But…I guess there were times before when I did well on other exams. It’s just hard to remember those when I’m panicking.
It sounds like the current experiences are overshadowing your previous successes. Let's consider when you've done well before – can you describe a time when you succeeded in your academic work?
There was a biology test last semester that I aced. I studied hard and felt confident going in. But now it seems like that was just a fluke.
It’s interesting that you were able to succeed before. What were you doing differently at that time compared to now?
I guess I wasn’t as stressed out. I believed in myself and my ability to understand the material. Now, it just feels impossible.
It seems like your self-belief played a big role in your past success. Do you think it might be worth exploring ways to challenge the current negative beliefs you have about your abilities?
I don’t know. It’s hard to imagine thinking differently when everything feels so overwhelming.

It’s understandable to feel that way, especially when it feels like these thoughts have such a strong hold on you. What if we took small steps to gently challenge these beliefs and consider alternative outcomes?
I guess that could help. But what kind of small steps?

Maybe we can start by identifying one specific negative thought, like “I’m going to fail,” and examining it more closely. We can look for evidence for and against this thought and then see if we can find a more balanced perspective. How does that sound?
It sounds tough, but I’m willing to try. I don’t want to keep feeling like this.

That sounds like a good beginning. Let’s try it with one specific thought, and we’ll work through it together. Over time, this practice might help you see things in a more realistic and less overwhelming way.
Okay, let’s do it. I really hope this can help me move past these feelings.
I believe that with time and practice, you can start to see a change. Let’s take it one step at a time and see where it leads us.

interaction.content: Hi Brooklyn, thank you for coming in today. How are you feeling about our session?
Honestly, I'm not sure. I don't usually talk about my feelings, and I'm not convinced this will help.
That's completely understandable. It's not easy to open up, especially when you're feeling uncertain. Can you tell me a bit about what's been on your mind lately?
Well, I've been volunteering at a nursing home, and there's this elderly lady who doesn't seem to like me. It's really been bothering me.
That sounds challenging. It must be tough to feel that way in a place where you're trying to help others. How has this situation affected your volunteering experience overall?
It's made me feel like a failure, like I don't belong there. I can't stop thinking about it whenever I'm at the nursing home.
I'm sorry to hear that you're feeling this way. What do you think it is about this particular encounter that's causing such strong feelings for you?
I don't know. Maybe it's just that I try so hard to connect with everyone, and when someone doesn't like me, it feels personal.
It sounds like you care a lot about making connections and being helpful. When you feel that someone doesn't like you, it might feel like it's a reflection of your efforts. Is that right?
Yeah, exactly. I can't help but feel inadequate, like I'm not good enough.
Thank you for sharing that with me. It's important to acknowledge these feelings even when they're difficult. Can we explore some specific thoughts you have about this situation?
Sure, though I don't know how helpful it will be. I just keep thinking that I'm doing something wrong or that I'm just really bad at this.
It can be really overwhelming to feel like you're making mistakes or that you’re not capable. What evidence do you have that supports these thoughts you're having?
Well, she ignores me and doesn't seem to want to talk to me. That's got to mean something.
I see. And what evidence do you have that might contradict the idea that you're doing something wrong?
Um, I guess some of the other residents seem to like me. We've had good conversations, and they've thanked me for spending time with them.

That's a great observation. It seems like there are aspects of your volunteering experience where you do feel positively received. How might we explore the possibility that there could be other reasons for the elderly lady's behavior that aren't about you?
Maybe she's having a bad day or she's just not feeling well. But it's hard to accept that when it feels so personal.
Absolutely, it's hard to detach our feelings from others' reactions. What do you think might help you start to shift how you view these encounters?
I don't know. It just feels so ingrained to think negatively about myself in these situations.

That makes a lot of sense. Changing how we think is definitely a process. How would you feel about trying to challenge some of these negative thoughts, and perhaps seeing if there are more compassionate ways you could think about yourself?
I could try, but I've never been good at being kind to myself. It's easier to see my faults.

It can be tough, but it's certainly worth exploring. Sometimes, treating ourselves with the same kindness we show others can make a big difference. What do you think could be a small step toward practicing more self-compassion?
Maybe I could remind myself that I'm there to help and that some people do appreciate me. But I don't know if that will change how I feel.

It's definitely a step in the right direction. Small changes in how we think can add up over time. How do you feel about setting some realistic goals for your volunteering, focusing on the positive interactions you have?
I guess I could try that. Focusing on the people who appreciate me might help a bit.
That sounds like a constructive approach. Let's keep exploring this together and see if we can create a more balanced perspective of your experiences. How does that sound to you?
It sounds okay. I'll give it a try, but I'm still skeptical.
It's perfectly fine to feel skeptical. We're here to work through this at your pace. I'm glad you're open to trying. Let's continue to explore and see where this journey takes us.

interaction.content: Hi Scott, welcome. How can I assist you today?
Hi, I’ve been feeling really down lately, especially after a tough hiking trip I had this past summer.
I’m sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about what happened during that hike?
Sure. It was a really challenging hike, and I struggled to climb a mountain. I felt incapable and just couldn't keep up with others.
That sounds like a difficult experience. How have these feelings affected you since the hike?
Well, I’ve been avoiding physical activities altogether. I just feel so unfit and demotivated.
It seems like this experience has had a big impact on your confidence in your athletic abilities. Have you noticed any other areas of your life being affected by these feelings?
Not really. My job as a cook is fine, and my relationships haven’t been affected much. But I used to enjoy hiking and other physical activities, and now I’m just avoiding them.
I understand. It sounds like this has taken away something you used to enjoy. What were some of the activities you liked doing before?
Hiking was big for me. I used to go pretty often. I also liked running and biking, but now I just feel like I’m not cut out for it anymore.
I can see how that would be discouraging. Can you tell me more about what goes through your mind when you think about doing these activities now?
I keep telling myself that I’ll fail again and that I'm just not athletic enough. It feels like any effort would be pointless.
It sounds like you're dealing with a lot of self-doubt. When you think about your abilities, how do you define what being "athletic enough" means to you?
To me, being athletic means not struggling with these activities, being able to complete a hike without feeling like I might collapse.
That’s quite a high standard. Given that definition, it makes sense that you’re feeling the way you do. Have there been times in the past when you felt capable or successful in physical activities?
Yeah, there were many times I completed hikes and even enjoyed them. This one bad experience just seems to overshadow everything.
It’s interesting how one challenging experience can have such an impact. If you could go back to that hike and change something to make it feel more successful, what would you do differently?
Maybe I would prepare more, like training or choosing an easier trail. The trail was pretty tough and I wasn’t in the best shape.
So there are factors other than your athletic ability that could have played a role, like preparation and trail difficulty. Does it help to think about it that way?
Yeah, I guess it does. It wasn’t just me being incapable; there were other things that made it harder.
Exactly. Thinking about those other factors, how do you feel about trying a different, perhaps easier, physical activity now?
I feel a bit anxious, but maybe it wouldn’t be so bad if I started with something manageable.
It’s understandable to feel anxious. What’s something small and manageable that you might be willing to try?
I could start with a short walk in the park. That’s not too intense, and I think I can handle it.
That sounds like a great starting point. How would you feel about setting that as a goal for this week?
I think I can do that. A short walk sounds achievable.
That’s wonderful. Taking small steps can help build your confidence. How do you plan to motivate yourself to take that walk?
I’ll remind myself how much I used to enjoy being active and that this is a step towards feeling good again.
That sounds like a solid plan. How do you feel about keeping track of your progress and reflecting on how it goes afterward?
I think that could be helpful. I’ll give it a try and see how I feel.
Great. Let’s reconvene and discuss how it went and any thoughts or feelings that came up. Does that sound good to you?
Yes, that sounds good. Thanks for your help.
You’re welcome, Scott. I look forward to hearing about your progress. Take care until then.

interaction.content: Hello Nathan, welcome. How are you feeling today?
Hi, I'm okay, I guess. Just really tired and frustrated with things at work.
I'm sorry to hear that. What’s been happening at work that's causing you to feel this way?
It's my students. They just don't behave as well as I expect them to. It's been really hard to manage them, and it's starting to get to me.
That sounds challenging. Can you tell me more about what specific behaviors are troubling you?
They don't listen, they mess around, and they just don't seem to respect me. I've tried different strategies, but nothing seems to work.
It seems like you’ve put in a lot of effort already. When did you start noticing these patterns of behavior?
Pretty much since I started this new job. It feels like it's gotten worse since I moved closer to the school, and I can’t stop comparing them to other kids I know.
The comparisons seem to be adding to your frustration. Can you give me an example of a time when this comparison felt particularly strong?
Sure, my friends’ children seem so polite and well-behaved. When I see them, I can’t help but feel disappointed and think "why can't my students be like that?"
It's understandable to feel disheartened, especially when you have an image of how things should be. When you have these thoughts, how do they affect your mood and interactions with your students?
I end up feeling more irritated and critical. I know it’s not fair to the kids, but it’s hard to hide my frustration.
It must be hard carrying that frustration daily. What have you been doing to try and manage these feelings?
I've tried different disciplinary strategies, but nothing really changes. I even tried talking to other teachers for advice, but I'm still stuck.
It sounds like you really care about doing a good job and have sought various solutions. How do you feel your students respond to your current methods?
Honestly, it seems like they don’t take me seriously. I feel like I’m not getting through to them at all.
That sense of not being effective can be really tough. Have you noticed any particular times or situations where your students respond more positively?
Sometimes, when we're doing something fun or hands-on, they lighten up, but those moments feel rare.
Those positive moments can be important. When you notice them, how do they impact your feelings about teaching?
They give me some hope, I guess. But then I think maybe I’m just not cut out for this if I can only connect with them during the 'easy' times.
It sounds like you're doubting your abilities because of these challenges. If we were to think about a time you felt successful as a teacher, what comes to mind?
There was a project last year where the kids were really engaged and excited. It felt great to see them learning and having fun.
That sounds like a rewarding experience. What do you think made that project different from your current challenges?
I think part of it was that I was more patient and creative with my approach. I was excited about the project, and it showed.
Your enthusiasm and patience seem to play significant roles in those successful moments. How might you bring some of that energy back into your current teaching environment?
Maybe if I can focus on finding more activities that engage them, I might feel better about their behavior. But it’s hard to stay positive when they’re acting up all the time.
It's understandable that maintaining a positive outlook can be difficult. How do you think your feelings of frustration impact your students’ behavior?
They probably pick up on my frustration and act out even more, which just makes everything worse.
It’s insightful that you recognize this. Let's think about ways to break this cycle. How might you approach situations differently to foster a more positive environment?
Perhaps I could try to pay more attention to their good behavior, even if it’s small stuff. Maybe that would encourage them to behave better overall.
That sounds like a constructive approach. Recognizing their positive behaviors could help shift the dynamic you currently have. How would you feel about giving that a try this week?
I’m willing to give it a shot. I really want to improve things, for both me and the kids.

interaction.content: Hi, Lacey. Please feel free to share anything that's on your mind today. What's been bothering you?

Hi. Well, I have been feeling really bad about myself lately, especially after trying to cheer up my friend from Tanzania, who was feeling sad. I just feel like I'm a terrible friend because I couldn't comfort her properly.
It sounds like you're really upset about this situation with your friend. Could you tell me more about what happened and what specifically made you feel this way?

Sure. My friend was going through a hard time, and I tried to say things to make her feel better, but she seemed to get even more upset. Since then, I've been thinking that I just made things worse and that I'm not good at being supportive.
I understand how that could make you feel inadequate. When you think back on that interaction, what are some of the specific thoughts that come to mind about yourself?
I keep thinking I'm useless and that I failed her when she needed me the most. I feel like I'm a bad friend and that maybe I'm not good at helping people in general.
Those are some pretty harsh thoughts you're having about yourself. Do these thoughts come up only in this situation, or do you notice them in other parts of your life as well?
Mostly just with this situation, but sometimes I think about other times when I felt like I didn't do enough for people. It's like this incident brought up all those other feelings too.

It sounds like this incident with your friend has stirred up a lot of self-doubt for you. When you feel like this, do you ever try to remind yourself of times when you were supportive or did something good for others?
Not really. I just keep replaying my mistakes over and over in my head. It's hard to focus on the positive when I feel so bad about messing up.

That makes sense. Sometimes, when we're feeling down, our minds focus more on the negative experiences. Can we try looking at your interaction with your friend from a different perspective? What were you hoping to achieve when you were trying to cheer her up?
I just wanted her to feel better, to know that she wasn't alone and that I cared about her. But it didn't work out that way, and I feel like I failed.

I hear that you had good intentions and that your care for your friend is really important to you. Even though the outcome wasn't what you hoped for, could it be possible that your efforts still showed your friend that you cared?
Maybe. I did spend time with her and tried to listen to her, but I still think I said the wrong things.
It sounds like you're very focused on the words you used. Do you think there's only one right way to support a friend, or could there be different ways to show support?
I guess there could be different ways. But I still feel like if I had been better at it, she wouldn't have gotten more upset.

It's natural to feel responsible, but people's reactions can be influenced by many factors beyond our control. You mentioned that you spent time with her and listened to her. What other ways do you think you might have shown she mattered to you?
Well, I did try to comfort her with some personal stories and told her I'm here for her whenever she needs me. But I still wish I had done more.

It sounds like you genuinely tried to connect and be there for her. Sometimes, our best efforts may not immediately help someone feel better, but that doesn't mean they don't appreciate us. What do you think your friend might remember about your interaction in the long run?
She might remember that I tried to help. I hope she can see that I care about her, even if I didn't say the perfect things.

That’s a very compassionate reflection, Lacey. It seems like you're acknowledging the effort and intention you brought to the situation. How does it feel to think that your friend might see the care you intended to show?
It feels a bit better, actually. I guess it helps to remember that my intentions were good, even if the outcome wasn’t perfect.

I'm glad to hear that. It's important to recognize your intentions and effort. As we work through these feelings, we can continue exploring ways to acknowledge your strengths and constructive beliefs about yourself. How does that sound?
That sounds really helpful. I want to be able to see myself as a good friend and not let one incident make me doubt everything.

It's great to hear you're open to that. We'll focus on challenging those negative labels and creating a more balanced perspective together. Remember, one incident doesn't define your abilities or worth as a friend. Let's take it step by step.
Thank you. I really appreciate this approach. I'm feeling hopeful about working through this.
You're welcome, Lacey. Your willingness to explore and reflect shows a lot of strength. We'll continue building on these positive steps in our future sessions.

interaction.content: Hi Greg, thanks for coming in today. How are you feeling about being here?
Honestly, I’m not sure. I just know that I’ve been struggling a lot lately and I don’t know what else to do.
It’s completely okay to feel uncertain about this process. It sounds like you’ve been carrying a lot on your shoulders. Could you tell me a bit about what has been going on for you?
It’s the accident. Someone rear-ended me while I was driving my kids to one of their sporting events. Ever since then, I’ve felt like I’m a terrible driver and it’s affecting everything in my life.
That must have been a really stressful experience. It’s understandable to have these feelings after such an event. Can you tell me more about how this has been impacting your daily life?

Well, I’ve been avoiding driving whenever I can. My anxiety goes through the roof when I think about getting behind the wheel, especially with my kids in the car. It’s making it really hard to manage everything.

So the anxiety is really affecting your ability to drive and fulfill your responsibilities. It makes sense that this would be creating a lot of stress for you. What thoughts or feelings come up for you when you think about the accident?
I keep replaying it in my mind. I feel so guilty for putting my kids at risk. I can’t help but think that if I had been a better driver, this wouldn’t have happened.
It sounds like there’s a lot of self-blame and guilt associated with this incident. These feelings can be incredibly overwhelming. What has your daily routine been like since the accident?

Disrupted, to say the least. I avoid driving whenever possible, which means my husband and friends have had to step in a lot. It's caused a lot of tension at home, particularly with my husband. He thinks I’m overreacting, but I just can’t help it.
It seems like this situation has strained your relationship with your husband as well. That can add another layer of difficulty. What about your friends—do you talk to them about these feelings?

Not really. I mean, I have friends in book clubs and PTA meetings, but I haven’t shared anything about how I’ve been feeling. I don’t want them to think I’m falling apart over something that seems so trivial.

It can be challenging to open up about these feelings, especially when you fear judgment from others. It sounds like you’ve been carrying a lot of this burden on your own. Have you noticed any particular thoughts that come up frequently when you’re feeling overwhelmed?
Mostly that I’m a bad driver and a bad parent for putting my kids at risk. I feel like I’m just not competent enough to handle everything.
Those are really tough thoughts to deal with. When you think about those self-labels, what emotions come up for you?
Frustration and hopelessness, mostly. I just feel stuck and don't know how to move forward.

Feeling stuck can be quite debilitating. It sounds like these thoughts are really tied to your sense of self-worth and competence. What do you think would change if you were able to view the accident from a different perspective?
I don’t know. Maybe I’d feel less guilty, but it’s hard to see how that can even happen when the incident keeps playing in my head.
It sounds like shifting your perspective on this event feels really difficult right now. What do you think it would take for you to start considering a different viewpoint?
I guess I’d need to see some concrete evidence that it wasn’t my fault—or that I’m not a bad driver because of one incident. But how do you even begin to do that?

That’s a great question, Greg. We can start by looking at the facts surrounding the accident and compare them with your current thoughts. This will help us determine if the labels you’re using are accurate. How does that sound to you?
It sounds a bit daunting, but I guess it makes sense. I’m willing to try if it means I might stop feeling this way.

I’m glad to hear that you’re open to exploring this further. As we go through this process, we’ll also look for strengths and positive actions you’ve taken that you might be overlooking. Do you remember any moments where you handled things well, even if they seem small?
I guess I made sure the kids were okay right after the accident. I kept calm for their sake, even though I was panicking inside.

That’s significant, Greg. Despite your anxiety, you prioritized your children’s safety and managed to remain calm externally. This shows you do have the ability to handle stressful situations. How does it feel to acknowledge that?
It’s hard to accept. Part of me feels a little better remembering that, but another part still blames myself for the whole thing.

It’s completely normal to have mixed feelings when you start reflecting on these events from a different angle. We’ll take this step by step. For now, let’s focus on that moment where you did something positive. Can you see how that challenges the idea that you’re a bad driver or parent?
A little bit, yeah. I can see that part of what happened wasn’t entirely terrible, but it’s not easy to let go of the guilt.

It’s a process, and it’s okay to take it one step at a time. Let’s continue to explore these thoughts and the evidence around them, and see if we can build a more balanced view. Would that be alright with you?
Yeah, let’s do that. It’s a start, at least.

interaction.content: Hi Paul, welcome. I'm glad you decided to come today. How are you feeling right now?
I'm feeling a bit nervous to be honest, but I'm here because I know I need help.
It's completely okay to feel nervous, Paul. Let's take it one step at a time. Can you tell me a bit about what's been troubling you recently?

It's this overwhelming guilt and fear I've been carrying since this incident at the circus. I was dressed as a clown, and I accidentally scared a lot of kids. Ever since then, I feel like my employer won't trust me again.
I see. It sounds like this incident has had a significant impact on you. Can you walk me through what happened that day?

Well, I was performing, and something went wrong. I tripped and fell close to the kids in the audience, and they got really scared. I tried to make it better, but I could see the looks on their faces and their parents' faces. It was awful.
That sounds like a tough situation, Paul. It makes sense that you would feel unsettled by it. What happened after the show? Did you speak to your employer or the parents?
Yeah, I apologized to the parents and the kids, and I thought it would make me feel better, but it didn’t. I just kept thinking that my employer would never trust me again because of this.
So even after you took steps to apologize, these feelings of guilt and fear remained. Is that right?
Exactly. And it's just gotten worse over time. I keep worrying about my reputation and what people think of me.
It sounds like these thoughts are quite persistent. Are there certain situations or places that trigger these feelings more intensely?
Definitely. Anytime I'm around children or when I'm at work, it just comes flooding back. I also think about it a lot when I'm alone.
It seems like these feelings are affecting various aspects of your life, including your work and personal time. How has this been impacting your daily activities and relationships?

It’s been really hard. I can't sleep properly, and I’m always anxious. My performance on the reality TV show has been suffering because of it too. I don’t feel like I can trust my employer or colleagues anymore.
That must be incredibly challenging. It’s good that you’re recognizing how this is impacting you. Have you shared these feelings with any of your friends or family?
No, I haven't. I have a supportive network, but I just haven’t been able to talk about this particular issue with them. It's embarrassing, you know?

I understand that it can be difficult to open up about things that feel so personal. It sounds like you’re seeking to regain a sense of trust and normalcy in your life. What are your hopes for our sessions together?
I really hope to find a way to get past this guilt and fear. I don’t want these memories to control me anymore. I want to feel confident in my job and trust my colleagues again.

That’s a very positive and important goal, Paul. We can definitely work on strategies to help you achieve that. I would like to start by understanding more about how you think and feel when these moments of guilt and fear arise. Can you describe what goes through your mind?
When it happens, I immediately think that I'm a failure and that no one will ever trust me again. I worry that people see me as a joke or that I'll mess up again.

Those thoughts sound very distressing. It seems like they are quite powerful and take a significant toll on you. Let’s try to explore these thoughts together. When you think that no one will ever trust you again, what evidence comes to mind that supports or contradicts this belief?
Well, the kids were really scared, and I know my employer was not happy about the incident. But on the other hand, my employer has not fired me and still gives me chances to work.
That's an important observation. Despite the incident, your employer has continued to give you opportunities. What does that suggest to you about their level of trust in you?
I guess it means that they still have some level of trust in me. Otherwise, I wouldn't still be working there.
Exactly. It seems like there might be more evidence that supports you being trusted than initially meets the eye. How does considering this perspective change the way you feel about your situation?
It makes me feel a bit more hopeful. Maybe I’m being too hard on myself and not seeing the full picture.

It's possible that you're focusing more on the negative aspects and underestimating the positives. Let's continue to explore these patterns and work on finding a balance that helps you feel more confident and less controlled by these negative thoughts.
That sounds like a good plan. I'm ready to start working on this.
Great, Paul. We'll take it step by step. You’re already showing a lot of resilience by facing these feelings and seeking help. Let’s build on that and find a path to feeling better.

interaction.content: Hello Nicholas, and welcome. I'm glad you're here. How can I assist you today?
Hi, thanks for having me. I've been feeling really disappointed and dissatisfied since finishing a book last week. The ending was terrible, and it's ruined reading for me.
That sounds really frustrating. Can you tell me more about what happened with the book and how it affected you?
Sure. I had high hopes for this book, and I was enjoying it a lot, but the ending was just awful. It made me feel like all the time I spent reading it was wasted.
I can understand why that would be upsetting. How often do these feelings come up for you since finishing the book?
Quite often, honestly. Every time I think about reading another book, I get anxious and worried that the same thing will happen.
It sounds like this experience has had a significant impact on your enjoyment of reading. How has this affected your daily life?
Reading used to be my way to relax and unwind. Now, I'm avoiding books altogether, and it's left me feeling stressed and without my usual form of escape.
It must be challenging to deal with those feelings, especially when reading was such an important part of your routine. Do you find yourself thinking about this specific book ending frequently?
Yes, every time I think about starting a new book, I remember how disappointed I was with the last one. It makes me hesitant to even pick up another book.
It sounds like a lot of your focus is on that negative experience. What were some of the things you enjoyed about reading before this happened?
I loved getting lost in different stories and characters. It was my way to relax and escape from daily stresses. I enjoyed the anticipation of what would happen next.
Those sound like very positive aspects of reading. When you think about those enjoyable parts, how do they compare to the negative feelings you have about the ending of that one book?
It's tricky. The good parts seem overshadowed by the bad ending. It feels like the negative experience just weighs more heavily on me.
It can be hard when one negative experience takes over the positive ones. Have you considered why the ending of this particular book had such a strong impact on you?
I think it's because I had such high expectations. I invested a lot of time and emotion into the story, and the ending just felt like a letdown. Like the journey was worthless.

Your feelings are valid, and it’s understandable why you’d feel that way with such high expectations. What if we take some time to explore these thoughts and try to look at them from a different angle?
I'm open to that. I just don't know where to start.
How about we begin with identifying the specific thoughts that come up when you think about reading a new book. What goes through your mind?
Usually, I think, "What if the ending is terrible?" or "What if I waste my time again?" It feels risky to invest time when I'm afraid of being disappointed.
Those are important thoughts to recognize. Let's consider the evidence for and against these thoughts. Have all your previous reading experiences had disappointing endings?
No, not all of them. Actually, most books I've read had pretty good endings. It’s just this last one that really threw me off.
That’s noteworthy. By acknowledging that most of your reading experiences were positive, does it change how you view the potential outcomes of reading a new book?
I suppose it does. It reminds me that not every book will have a bad ending. But it's still hard to shake that fear.

It's understandable that the fear is still there. What if we reframe your thought about potentially disappointing endings? Can you think of a way to phrase it that incorporates your past positive experiences?
Maybe something like, "Even if I don't like the ending, I can still enjoy the rest of the book," or "Most books have good endings, so it's worth giving it a try."
Those are great reframes. They acknowledge the possibility of disappointment but also remind you of the enjoyment you typically get from reading.
Yeah, I can see how that could help. It takes away some of the absolute fear of disappointment.

Exactly. It can be helpful to remind yourself of the overall positive experiences you’ve had with reading. How about we practice this reframing over the next week and see how it affects your thoughts about reading?
That sounds like a good idea. I think I could try that and see if it makes a difference.
Great. We'll discuss how it goes in our next session. Remember, changing thought patterns takes time and practice, so be patient with yourself.
Thanks, I'll keep that in mind. I appreciate the help.
You're welcome, Nicholas. I’m here to support you through this process. See you next time.

interaction.content: Hi Geoffrey, I’m glad you could make it today. How are you feeling right now?
Honestly, not great. I’ve been feeling pretty down and questioning a lot about myself recently.
I'm sorry to hear that. Can you share a bit more about what's been going on that's making you feel this way?
Well, it all started after my wife left me. Since then, I’ve been struggling, especially with my work. I recently lost my first case in court, and I just feel like a complete failure.
That sounds really tough. It makes sense that losing a case, on top of your recent separation, would feel overwhelming. Can you tell me more about how these experiences are affecting you day-to-day?
I just keep thinking I’m the worst lawyer ever. Every mistake I make feels like more evidence that I can’t do my job. It’s hard to focus on anything else.
It sounds like these thoughts are really taking a toll on your confidence and your work. When you think about being "the worst lawyer ever," what specifically comes to mind?
I think about how I lost that case and how I must have looked so incompetent in front of everyone in the courtroom. It's like, if I can't even win one case, what does that say about me as a lawyer?
I can see why losing the case would bring up those kinds of thoughts. Have these kinds of thoughts always been there or did they start more recently?
They started after the divorce. Before that, I never really questioned my abilities this much. But the loss of the case made everything worse. Now it’s like a constant weight.
I understand that it can be hard to shake off these thoughts, especially when they're so persistent. Have you noticed any patterns or particular situations when these thoughts are strongest?
Usually when I’m at work or when I’ve had a setback. Even when I try to distract myself by running, the thoughts just keep coming back.
It seems like work-related setbacks are a major trigger for these thoughts. You mentioned you engage in running to cope. How helpful has running been for you in these moments?
Running helps a bit in the moment, but the relief is temporary. The negative thoughts just find their way back right after.

It sounds like running provides a short break, but doesn't address the core issue. Let’s take a closer look at one of these thoughts. For example, what evidence do you have that you're the worst lawyer ever?
I lost the case. I mean, that’s pretty big evidence, isn’t it? Plus, my performance has been slipping in general since the divorce.
Losing a case is definitely challenging, but does one case define your entire career and abilities as a lawyer?
Maybe not, but it feels like it does. When something like this happens, it overshadows everything else.
It seems like a lot of weight is being put on this one event. Are there any instances where you felt competent or successful in your job, even if they were small moments?
I guess there were times in the past when I did well in court or received positive feedback from clients, but those seem so far away now.
Those moments are still part of your professional journey. It’s important to remember them. How might looking at these positive instances challenge the way you currently see yourself?
It’s hard to even think about the positives when the negatives are so glaring, but I suppose there were times when I felt like I did a good job.
Acknowledging those moments can be a step towards seeing a more balanced perspective. How willing are you to explore these positive experiences further?
I guess I could try. It’s hard to see the positive, but I’m willing to give it a shot.
That’s a good start. Together, we can work on recognizing these moments and gradually shifting the focus away from the negatives. How does that sound?
It sounds difficult, but I think I need to try something different. My current mindset isn’t working for me.
It may be challenging, but taking these steps could help lighten the weight of these negative thoughts. Let’s continue to explore ways to achieve a more balanced perspective moving forward. Shall we?
Yeah, let’s do that. I need to break out of this cycle, and I’m ready to try.
